slides.title: Real Numbers
slides.speaker_notes: Sharper view of integers, rationals, irrationals.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Apply Euclid's lemma + algorithm to find HCF.
Use prime factorisation to find HCF and LCM.
Decide if a fraction has a terminating decimal.

slides.title: Euclid's division lemma
bullets: For positive integers a, b: a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b.

slides.title: Euclid's division algorithm
bullets: To find HCF(a, b): apply the lemma to (a, b), then (b, r₁), then (r₁, r₂), …
Faster than listing factors for large numbers.

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
bullets: Every composite number has a unique prime factorisation (up to order).
Once you have factorisations, HCF/LCM is mechanical.

slides.title: HCF and LCM by factorisation
bullets: HCF: SMALLEST power of each prime appearing in BOTH factorisations.
LCM: LARGEST power of EVERY prime appearing in EITHER.
Identity: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b.
Use it as a shortcut when you know three of the four.

slides.title: Three-number HCF and LCM
slides.speaker_notes: Generalises to any number of integers.

slides.title: Irrational numbers
bullets: Their decimal expansions are non-terminating, non-repeating.

slides.title: Proof: √2 is irrational
bullets: Write p = 2k. Then q² = 2k² → q is even.
Both p, q even — contradicts lowest terms!

slides.title: Combining rationals and irrationals
bullets: Be careful — sums/products of two irrationals are not always irrational.

slides.title: Rational numbers and their decimals
bullets: Every rational has either a TERMINATING decimal or a NON-TERMINATING REPEATING decimal.
A rational p/q (lowest terms) terminates iff q = 2^m · 5^n.
Examples: 7/8 → terminates (8=2³). 23/30 → does NOT (30 has a 3).

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. In a = bq + r, what's the constraint on r?

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Euclid's lemma: a = bq + r, 0 ≤ r < b.
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: unique prime factorisation.
√2, √3, π are irrational; proof by contradiction.
Rational p/q terminates ↔ q = 2^m · 5^n; # digits = max(m, n).
